planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in spring or fall.

directions: Press rooted offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun, barely covering the roots. Native to the mountains of Turkey and the wider Caucasus region, this species forms small, tight rosettes of gray-green leaves that often take on reddish tips under strong light and dry conditions. It spreads slowly by offsets to form a dense mat, tolerates poor rocky soil and drought once established, and is well suited to a scree bed, trough, or crevice garden alongside other alpine Sempervivum species. Water only during extended dry spells and avoid any soil that holds moisture around the crown.

common_name: Large-Flowered Hens and Chicks (Resinous Alpine Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in spring or fall.

directions: Plant offsets in very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates. Native to the Western Alps of France, Switzerland, and Italy, this species forms medium rosettes of sticky, glandular-hairy, yellow-green leaves that release a strong resinous or goat-like odor when bruised, a trait unique among commonly grown hens and chicks. It is also one of the few Sempervivum species with pale yellow rather than pink or red flowers, produced on short stalks in summer before the flowering rosette dies back and leaves its offsets to continue the clump. Grow in rock gardens, troughs, or gravel beds where its unusual scent and color can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings or container stock in fall or spring in well-drained, sandy-loam soil.

directions: Plant stem cuttings or container stock in well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun to partial shade. Native to Tenerife and La Palma in the Canary Islands, this shrubby, winter-growing Aeonium forms small, slightly sticky rosettes of pale green leaves on branching stems, topped by clusters of star-shaped yellow flowers. Like other aeoniums it grows actively through the cool, moist winter months and rests during hot, dry summers, so taper watering back once summer heat arrives. Grow in a container or rock garden where it can be moved under cover before frost in climates colder than zone 9.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings or container stock in fall or spring in well-drained, sandy-loam soil.

directions: Plant stem cuttings in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun. Native to the arid eastern Canary Islands of Lanzarote and Fuerteventura, this is one of the more drought-adapted, shrubbier aeoniums, developing a woody, branching framework topped with loose rosettes of narrow gray-green leaves rather than the broad flat rosettes typical of the genus. The common name refers to the resinous, balsam-like sap the stems exude when cut, which Canary Island residents have historically used in folk remedies. Give it the driest, sunniest spot available and protect from frost and prolonged winter wet.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in well-drained soil in spring after the last frost.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this low groundcover stonecrop forms a dense mat of tiny, rounded, chartreuse-yellow leaves that pack tightly together into ball-like clusters along creeping stems. Color is brightest in full sun and fades toward green in heavier shade or cooler weather. It spreads readily by rooting along the stems, making it useful for filling gaps between pavers, cascading over container edges, or carpeting a rock garden alongside other small-leaved sedums. Water sparingly once established and avoid soggy soil, which quickly causes rot.
sources: Mountain Crest Gardens — Sedum Cultivar Guide

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring in well-drained, average garden soil.

directions: Divide clumps in spring and plant in well-drained, average to lean garden soil in full sun. This older, compact German border stonecrop holds fleshy, bronze-purple to deep red-brown foliage all season on sturdy, upright stems, with flattened clusters of pink-red flowers opening in late summer that age toward rust as they dry. Its smaller stature compared to 'Autumn Fire' or 'Herbstfreude' makes it useful near the front of a sunny border or in a large container without flopping. Leave the dried flower heads standing into winter for structure and interest, then cut back and divide every few years as the clump thins in the center.

planting.note: Pot up offsets or nursery divisions in fast-draining succulent mix any time in the growing season.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container succulent in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix. Native to South Africa's Eastern Cape, this species forms a low, dense rosette of thick, firm, recurved leaves with a rough, somewhat warty texture in muted olive-green to grayish-brown tones, a notably somber coloring compared to the brighter banded Haworthiopsis species. It stays small and slow-growing, making it well suited to a windowsill or shallow succulent dish. Water only once the soil has dried fully and avoid intense direct afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaves.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot up offsets in a shallow dish in fast-draining succulent mix any time in the growing season.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a shallow pot of fast-draining, gritty succulent mix. One of the smallest species in the genus, native to the Eastern Cape of South Africa, it forms tight clusters of tiny rosettes rarely more than an inch across, with short, triangular, grayish-green leaves that carry faint translucent tips. It offsets readily to form a dense miniature colony over time, making it a good choice for a small dish garden or windowsill collection of dwarf succulents. Water sparingly and let the mix dry completely between waterings to avoid rot in its small root system.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock after last frost in well-drained soil.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Native to southern Africa and Mozambique, this shrubby succulent is grown for its rounded, scalloped leaves held on distinctly six-angled stems, which flush a rich copper-red to burgundy color under strong sun and bright light and stay greener in shade. Small clusters of yellow flowers appear in winter on mature plants grown outdoors in mild climates. In colder regions grow it in a container that can be moved indoors before frost, and pinch growing tips to keep the naturally leggy habit more compact.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix; best grown in a hanging basket.

directions: Grow in bright light in fast-draining succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried fully. Native to Madagascar, this species has weak, slender, trailing stems clothed in small, narrow leaves and produces slim, tubular, orange-red flowers that dangle from the stem tips, most freely in late winter and spring. Its sprawling, pendent habit is far better suited to a hanging basket than an upright pot, where the flowers can hang clear of the foliage for display. It is one of the parent species behind the popular hybrid Kalanchoe 'Tessa', already documented in this dataset; pinch spent flowering stems to keep growth tidy and encourage fuller rebloom.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
